what_its_for: Triazolam is a sleep medicine used to treat short-term insomnia (trouble falling asleep or staying asleep). It helps you fall asleep faster and sleep through the night. It is usually only used for 7 to 10 days at a time.
how_to_take: Take triazolam exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Take it right before you get into bed, only when you are ready to sleep for a full 7 to 8 hours. Do not take it if you will need to wake up earlier than that. Never take more than your prescribed dose. Do not crush or chew the tablet.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 0.125 mg to 0.25 mg taken at bedtime. Older adults (over 65) are usually started on a lower dose of 0.125 mg to lower the risk of falls and confusion. Never take more than 0.5 mg in one night. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
missed_dose: If you forget to take your dose at bedtime, skip it if it is almost time to wake up. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. Only take triazolam when you have a full night (7 to 8 hours) to sleep.
storage: Store triazolam at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep it out of the reach of children. Do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of any unused medicine properly — ask your pharmacist about medication take-back programs.
what_to_avoid: Do NOT drink alcohol while taking triazolam — this can cause dangerous drowsiness, breathing problems, or even death. Avoid other sleep medicines, anxiety medicines, or opioid pain medicines unless your doctor approves them. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires you to be fully alert the morning after taking triazolam, as drowsiness can linger. Avoid eating grapefruit or drinking grapefruit juice, as it can increase the amount of this drug in your body and cause stronger side effects. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor if you have been using it for a while.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: unusual sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking, sleep-driving, or doing other activities while not fully awake; confusion, aggression, or strange behavior; memory loss (amnesia) the morning after taking the medicine; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing; thoughts of harming yourself; or if your sleep problems do not improve or get worse after 7 to 10 days.
when_it_works: Triazolam works quickly. Most people start to feel sleepy within 15 to 30 minutes of taking it. It is a fast-acting medicine but does not stay in your body for a long time, which is why it works best for helping you fall asleep. It should only be used for short periods (no more than 1 to 2 weeks).
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): Use a lower dose (0.125 mg) because older adults are more sensitive to this medicine and have a higher risk of falls, confusion, and memory problems. Pregnancy: Do NOT take triazolam if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It can harm the unborn baby. Breastfeeding: Do not use triazolam while breastfeeding, as it can pass into breast milk and harm the baby. Liver or kidney problems: Tell your doctor if you have liver or kidney disease, as this medicine may build up in your body and cause stronger effects. Children: Triazolam is NOT approved for use in children under 18 years of age.
